query: High-entropy alloys can combine mechanical strength, wear resistance, corrosion protection, oxidation resistance, and thermal stability, while their large compositional space offers opportunities to tune degradation in harsh environments. Prior studies have largely considered wear and corrosion separately, and only a few reports address their combined action, leaving the governing behavior poorly understood. For a high-entropy alloy subjected to tribo-corrosion, what single mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs the coupled response and why? Describe a controlled comparison that would isolate the governing cause, predict changes in total degradation and its wear and corrosion components relative to a matched baseline, state where the prediction should hold or fail, connect it to the available prior evidence, and identify a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Fine-grained equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi HEA develops a uniform, rapidly re-passivating passive oxide film that reduces overall tribo-corrosion degradation. Specifically, the fine-grained sample is expected to show at least a 25% reduction in combined wear-corrosion mass loss and a decrease in friction coefficient by approximately 0.1 compared to its coarse-grained counterpart.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi HEA prepared with controlled processing to yield either fine-grained (enhanced grain boundary density) or coarse-grained microstructures.
generation.intervention: Apply thermomechanical processing to one set of samples to achieve significant grain refinement while maintaining composition, leaving a matched set as coarse-grained controls.
generation.conditions: Tribocorrosion tests in a 3.5 wt% NaCl solution under identical sliding conditions with moderate loads where re-passivation kinetics can effectively compete with film rupture.
generation.structural_mediator: Increased grain boundary density in fine-grained samples accelerates oxide nucleation, leading to the formation of a uniform, self-healing passive film that mitigates local corrosion and stabilizes friction behavior.
generation.mechanism: Grain refinement enhances the density of nucleation sites for passive oxide formation, promoting rapid re-passivation after wear-induced disruption. This robust and uniform oxide film reduces both the rate of anodic metal dissolution and the mechanical wear caused by friction.
generation.predicted_outcome: Fine-grained HEA samples will exhibit a lower steady-state friction coefficient (by approximately 0.1 units) and at least 25% lower total mass loss from combined tribo-corrosion compared to coarse-grained samples.
generation.baseline: Coarse-grained CoCrFeMnNi HEA samples tested under identical sliding and corrosion conditions.
generation.boundary: This prediction holds at moderate loads and sliding speeds allowing for effective oxide re-passivation; under extreme loads or high speeds that overwhelm film recovery, the benefit may diminish.
generation.uncertainty: Although the qualitative effect of grain refinement is well supported, the precise quantitative reduction in mass loss and friction may depend on operating conditions such as load intensity, sliding speed, and electrolyte concentration.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate HEA samples with significantly refined grain sizes and compare them with coarse-grained samples under identical tribo-corrosion conditions. Monitor OCP, friction coefficient, and cumulative mass loss over time.
measurements: Interferometric wear volume or mass loss determination
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the fine-grained samples do not show at least a 25% reduction in combined mass loss and a reduction in friction coefficient by ~0.1 compared to the coarse-grained samples, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: This work studied an equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi high entropy alloy that was manufactured using a laser-based consolidation additive manufacturing process. We showed that low friction and high wear resistance are achievable with bare high entropy alloys in inert environments. These characteristics are linked to the shear-induced formation of a highly refined, near-amorphous surface film that exhibits inverse Hall-Petch behavior. The detrimental role of environments, specifically those that result in oxidation, was mitigated by tribological testing in a UHV environment. A newly proposed amorphization model was used to accurately predict the grain size-dependent shear strength, and thus friction coefficient.

papers.title: Investigation of surface hardness, thermostability, tribo-corrosion, and microstructural morphological properties of microwave-synthesized high entrop
papers.system: Fe20Co20Ni20Mn20Cu20 HEA cladded on SS-304 steel
papers.approach: Microwave cladding with subsequent thermal exposure (up to 800 °C) and morphological evaluation (corrosion and wear behavior)
papers.findings: Thermal treatment promoted the formation of protective oxide layers (e.g., Cr2O3 and high-entropy spinel phases) that reduce corrosion rates and alter wear patterns; surface hardness increases and microstructural evolution contributes to improved resistance under tribo-corrosion conditions.
papers.mechanism: A dynamic passive oxide film forms during thermal exposure that acts as both a barrier against corrosive species and a mediator for wear by modifying surface roughness and friction, but can be disrupted by mechanical stresses.

papers.title: Study on cavitation erosion-corrosion behavior of CoCrFeNiMoCu0.1 high entropy alloy in 3.5 wt% NaCl solution.
papers.system: CoCrFeNiMoCu0.1 HEA in a 3.5 wt% NaCl solution under cavitation erosion (CE) conditions
papers.approach: Electrochemical testing (OCP shifts, potentiodynamic polarization) coupled with cyclic cavitation erosion to quantify mass loss and separate mechanical and corrosion contributions
papers.findings: A four-stage OCP evolution was observed with initial passive film protection, followed by film breakdown and re-passivation; the synergistic interaction (CE-induced corrosion and corrosion-induced CE) contributed to roughly 48% of the total mass loss.
papers.mechanism: The coupled degradation arises from the balance between passive film stability (which suppresses anodic dissolution) and its mechanical rupture under CE, leading to accelerated local corrosion when the film is compromised.

papers.title: Self-Lubricating Tribo-Catalytic Activity of 2D High Entropy Alloy Nanoflakes.
papers.approach: Ball‐on‐disk tribological experiments under high contact pressures combined with multi‐scale characterizations and molecular dynamic simulations
papers.findings: Demonstrated extremely low friction coefficients and wear rates under high pressures in ambient conditions due to stress‐induced transformation; the self-lubricating and tribo-catalytic behavior extends lubricant lifespan at the sliding interface.
papers.mechanism: Under sliding shear, the HEA nanoflakes undergo tribocatalytic processes that trigger the in situ formation of a lubricious, ultra-nanocrystalline surface layer, reducing friction and wear.

papers.title: Enhanced Wear and Corrosion Resistance of AlCoCrFeNiMoTi High-Entropy Alloy via B Addition by Laser Cladding.
papers.system: AlCoCrFeNiMoTiBx HEA coatings on Q235 steel with varying B content
papers.approach: Laser cladding with controlled boron microalloying, supported by SEM/EDS microstructural analysis, tribological testing, and electrochemical polarization/EIS measurements
papers.findings: Optimal boron addition (x ≈ 0.5–1) refines the BCC microstructure and promotes the in situ formation of TiB2, which simultaneously enhances wear resistance (by increasing hardness) and improves corrosion resistance (by stabilizing a passive film). Excessive B leads to TiB2 agglomeration, generating defects in the passive layer.
papers.mechanism: The interplay between mechanical reinforcement (via TiB2-induced lattice distortion) and passive film integrity controls tribo-corrosion; improved passive film formation mitigates corrosive attack while enhancing wear resistance.

papers.title: Effect of Thermal Shock on Properties of a Strongly Amorphous AlCrTiZrMo High-Entropy Alloy Film.
papers.system: AlCrTiZrMo HEA film subjected to varied thermal annealing (400–800 °C) in air
papers.approach: Thermal shock annealing at different temperatures combined with in situ tribocorrosion testing (monitoring OCP and COF), complemented by microstructural and compositional analyses
papers.findings: Annealing at 800 °C results in the in situ formation of a dense composite oxide (ZrTiO4) that significantly enhances tribocorrosion resistance by reducing ΔOCP and COF fluctuations and lowering wear rate, compared to films annealed at lower temperatures.
papers.mechanism: High-temperature-induced passive oxide layer formation improves re-passivation and barrier properties during friction-corrosion; the dense oxide layer limits both mechanical wear and corrosive attack.

papers.title: Effect of Grain Size on the Tribological Behavior of CoCrFeMnNi High Entropy Alloy.
papers.system: Equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy alloy with fine-grained (FG) versus coarse-grained (CG) microstructures
papers.approach: Sliding wear experiments under varying loads and speeds combined with SEM characterization of worn tracks; friction coefficient and wear rate measurements
papers.findings: Fine-grained samples exhibit formation of more uniform and durable oxide (glaze) layers that act as lubrication films, leading to lower friction coefficients and improved wear resistance compared to coarse-grained samples, which display pronounced plastic deformation and fragmented oxide layers.
papers.mechanism: Grain refinement promotes formation and stability of protective oxide films that mediate the coupled response by serving as both a barrier to corrosion and a lubricating interface to reduce wear.

papers.title: Evidence of Inverse Hall-Petch Behavior and Low Friction and Wear in High Entropy Alloys.
papers.system: Equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi HEA tested in inert ultra-high vacuum (UHV) environments
papers.approach: Sliding friction experiments in UHV combined with high-resolution STEM analysis of dynamically formed near-surface layers
papers.findings: A near-amorphous, ultra-nanocrystalline surface layer forms during shear which correlates with a reduced friction coefficient; results support an inverse Hall-Petch behavior where decreasing grain size leads to lower shear strength.
papers.mechanism: The mechanically activated formation of an ultra-fine, amorphous surface film lowers friction under inert conditions; while this mechanism benefits wear resistance, its role under tribocorrosion (where oxidation is relevant) needs to be integrated with passive film behavior.

papers.title: Titanium-induced phase changes and tribological behavior in cantor-based high entropy alloys.
papers.system: Cantor-based HEA with intentional titanium additions
papers.approach: Experimental examination of tribological performance in relation to titanium-induced phase modifications
papers.findings: Ti additions trigger phase changes that can modify the alloy’s microstructure, thereby influencing friction and wear properties; the phase stability directly affects mechanical and tribocorrosion performance.
papers.mechanism: Titanium acts to stabilize certain phases that promote a balanced formation of passive films and mechanical robustness, which is critical under tribocorrosion conditions.

papers.title: Effect of B Content on Microstructure and Properties of CrFeNiAlSi High-Entropy Alloys.
papers.system: CrFeNiAlSiBx HEAs exposed to high-temperature oxidation
papers.approach: Oxidation tests over 100 hours at 800 °C with varying levels of boron content, combined with morphological characterization of oxide layers
papers.findings: Low boron content enhances the formation of uniform, protective oxide scales that mitigate oxidation, while excessive B leads to oxide film defects; this balance is critical for both wear and corrosion protection.
papers.mechanism: Boron addition tunes the antioxidant activity by modifying the formation and stability of the passive oxide layer, which in turn influences the alloy’s resistance to tribologically induced degradation.

established: Protective passive oxide film formation is key to mitigating both corrosion and wear in HEAs.
Microstructural factors such as grain size, phase distribution, and alloying additions (e.g., B, Ti) strongly influence passive film stability and mechanical properties.
Mechanical actions (such as friction and cavitation) continuously disrupt passive films, while environmental exposure (thermal, chemical) drives re-passivation.

approaches_tried.approach: Microwave or laser cladding to deposit HEA coatings with controlled microstructures
approaches_tried.outcome: Enhanced wear and corrosion resistance via formation of protective oxide layers; success depends on processing parameters and alloying additions.

approaches_tried.approach: Thermal annealing or thermal shock to induce in situ passive film formation
approaches_tried.outcome: Improved tribocorrosion performance when dense oxide layers (e.g., ZrTiO4) are formed; performance degrades if oxide layers are fragmented.

approaches_tried.approach: Electrochemical testing under simulated cavitation erosion conditions
approaches_tried.outcome: Quantification of synergistic degradation; established that passive film breakdown under mechanical stress significantly enhances corrosion.

mechanisms: Dynamic balance between passive film formation (re-passivation) and mechanical disruption (wear-induced rupture) governs the coupled tribo-corrosion response.
Shear-induced surface amorphization and tribocatalysis can lower friction but may interact complexly with corrosion processes.
Alloying and microstructural control (via grain refinement, B or Ti additions) tune both mechanical strength and passive film stability.
disagreements: Some studies emphasize that oxide layers serve as effective lubricating films, while others suggest that defects or agglomeration in the passive film accelerate corrosion.
The relative contribution of mechanical wear versus corrosion-induced material loss varies with testing conditions (e.g., inert vs. corrosive environments) and remains debated.
open_questions: How does the in situ reformation rate of the passive film quantitatively balance with its mechanical removal under varying loads and environmental conditions?
What are the relative contributions of wear-induced mechanical damage and accelerated corrosion in different HEA systems during tribo-corrosion?
Under which precise operating conditions (load, temperature, electrolyte composition) does passive film stability become the dominant factor versus other degradation modes?
opportunities: Perform controlled comparisons between HEA samples with tailored passive film re-passivation capabilities (e.g., through minor alloying additions or thermal treatments) and baseline samples under identical tribo-corrosive conditions.
Develop in situ real-time monitoring (combining electrochemical noise with friction measurements) to correlate passive film integrity with overall degradation.

Explore novel alloy compositions that integrate mechanical reinforcement (via controlled grain size and phase distribution) with optimized passive film formation to minimize coupled wear and corrosion.

Investigate transitional regimes where the mechanistic shift from wear-dominated to corrosion-dominated degradation occurs; a clear deviation in this balance would falsify the passive film–governed hypothesis.

directions.direction: Control of grain size/microstructure to promote uniform and rapidly re-forming passive oxide films.
directions.assessment: Refining grains in HEAs (e.g., CoCrFeMnNi) is known to promote more uniform oxide layers that protect against both wear and corrosion. Prior studies [PMC9960858::web::019::3_4_worn_track_morphology_and_wear_mecha, PMC7311485::web::012::results_and_discussion] support the role of grain refinement. It directly addresses the coupled degradation by improving re-passivation kinetics and reducing mechanical damage. The approach is feasible using established thermomechanical processing.

directions.direction: Thermal processing to induce in situ formation of a dense composite oxide layer.
directions.assessment: Annealing HEA films (e.g., AlCrTiZrMo) at high temperature promotes formation of robust oxide phases (like ZrTiO4) that resist both corrosion and wear. Evidence in [PMC10456374::web::012::3_4_tribocorrosion_performance_after_ann, PMC10456374::web::008::3_2_high_temperature_annealing_in_air_en] supports this. It is a direct intervention that can be controlled, though sensitivity to processing parameters must be managed.

directions.direction: Minor alloying additions (e.g., boron) to refine microstructure and stabilize passive films.
directions.assessment: Adding a small amount of boron in HEA coatings (for example, AlCoCrFeNiMoTi) has been shown [PMC12565319::web::000::abstract] to refine microstructure and modify in situ TiB2 formation, which in turn stabilizes the passive film. This composite effect directly mitigates both wear and corrosion. The approach is supported by known intermetallic effects, though it requires carefully balancing B content.

directions.direction: Exploiting tribocatalytic behavior in 2D HEA nanoflakes to form an in situ lubricious surface layer.
directions.type: surface or coating and processing/synthesis route
directions.assessment: 2D HEA nanoflakes (e.g., (MoWNbTaV)0.2S2) have been demonstrated to undergo shear‐induced tribocatalytic transformations forming ultra-nanocrystalline, self-lubricating films [PMC12019924::web::000::abstract, PMC12019924::web::010::tribological_performance_of_2d_hea]. This mechanism couples mechanical protection with chemical passivation. It is an innovative route that may effectively decouple wear and corrosion, though its interplay with corrosive environments is less established and merits further study.

directions.direction: Real-time electrochemical-tribological monitoring to decouple and quantify the relative contributions of wear-induced film rupture and corrosion re-passivation kinetics.
directions.assessment: In situ combined measurements (e.g., monitoring OCP and friction coefficient) under tribo-corrosive conditions could reveal the dynamic balance between passive film rupture and reformation. This approach, while indirect, would inform mechanistic models and isolate key variables. Prior work [PMC10456374::web::012::3_4_tribocorrosion_performance_after_ann, PMC11378927::web::016::electrochemical_behavior_of_cocrfenimocu] provides baseline evidence. However, its complexity in signal deconvolution renders it less direct than the other four directions.

candidates.intervention: Introduce ~0.5 wt% B during the laser cladding process to produce modified coatings.

candidates.hypothesis: Under high contact pressure in a corrosive environment, (MoWNbTaV)0.2S2 2D HEA nanoflakes undergo shear‐induced tribocatalytic transformations that form an ultra-nanocrystalline, lubricious surface film. This film reduces friction by at least 20% and wear rates by around 30% while lowering corrosion rates, resulting in a significantly reduced total tribo-corrosion degradation compared to a bulk HEA without 2D nanoflake morphology.
candidates.intervention: Subject samples to controlled ball-on-disk sliding tests at high contact pressures (around 0.936 GPa) in a corrosive medium (3.5 wt% NaCl) while simultaneously monitoring friction and electrochemical parameters.
candidates.changes: Added quantitative predictions for friction and wear improvements; expanded the boundary conditions by specifying corrosive environment parameters and contact pressures; clarified that in situ tribocatalytic transformation evidence (e.g. from PMC12019924 evidence) supports the mechanism; recommended in situ spectroscopic characterization to directly monitor film evolution.

candidates.hypothesis: Fine-grained equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi HEA develops a uniform, rapidly re-passivating passive oxide film that reduces overall tribo-corrosion degradation. Specifically, the fine-grained sample is expected to show at least a 25% reduction in combined wear-corrosion mass loss and a decrease in friction coefficient by approximately 0.1 compared to its coarse-grained counterpart.
candidates.intervention: Apply thermomechanical processing to one set of samples to achieve significant grain refinement while maintaining composition, leaving a matched set as coarse-grained controls.
candidates.changes: Incorporated explicit quantitative predictions (e.g., 25% lower mass loss and decrease in friction coefficient by ~0.1 units) and clarified that enhanced passive film formation stems from increased grain boundary density. Specified boundary conditions regarding moderate loads and clarified uncertainties related to extreme loading conditions.

candidates.hypothesis: An AlCrTiZrMo HEA film annealed at 800 °C forms a dense, uniform ZrTiO4 composite oxide layer that enhances passive film integrity. This oxide layer leads to a reduction in friction coefficients by approximately 30% and wear rates by around 50%, while also stabilizing OCP by roughly 40 mV during tribo-corrosion tests relative to a non-annealed film.
candidates.intervention: Subject the film to thermal shock annealing at 800 °C for 1 hour in air to induce rapid, in situ oxide formation.
candidates.changes: Expanded the quantitative predictions (e.g., friction reduction by ~30%, wear rate reduction by ~50%, and OCP stabilization improvement of ~40 mV); provided clarification on the oxide composition confirmation via additional analyses (TEM, XPS); and specified load thresholds under which the composite oxide remains intact.

candidates.hypothesis: Incorporating approximately 0.5 wt% boron into AlCoCrFeNiMoTi HEA coatings stabilizes the passive film through microstructural refinement and the in situ formation of finely dispersed TiB2 particles. This stabilization reduces the synergistic effects of tribo-corrosion, leading to a reduction in corrosion current density by about 50% and a wear rate decrease of roughly 30% relative to B-free coatings.
candidates.intervention: Introduce ~0.5 wt% boron during the laser cladding process to obtain modified coatings with controlled microstructural refinement and in situ TiB2 formation.
candidates.changes: Enhanced the mechanistic explanation by detailing how in situ TiB2 formation contributes to passive film self-healing; provided justification for the 0.5 wt% B level based on prior observations; incorporated quantitative predictions (e.g., ~50% reduction in corrosion current density and ~30% reduction in wear rate) and clarified process control requirements.
